name: Deontology
statement: Some acts are right or wrong in themselves, by rule or duty, whatever consequences they produce.
statementAccent: right or wrong in themselves, by rule or duty
meaning: Deontology, or deontological ethics, is a class of normative ethical theories holding that the morality of an action depends on whether the action itself conforms to a moral rule, duty, or principle, rather than on its consequences. The name comes from the Greek deon, meaning duty. For a deontologist, some acts are right or wrong in themselves, so that certain actions, such as lying or killing the innocent, may be forbidden even when performing them would produce better consequences, and certain duties must be honored regardless of outcomes. Deontology is thus a duty-based or rule-based ethics, standing in opposition to consequentialism, which judges actions solely by their outcomes, and differing from virtue ethics, which centers on character. Deontological theories characteristically include constraints, prohibitions that hold even when violating them would produce more good, and often options or prerogatives that permit agents to pursue their own projects. The most famous deontologist is Immanuel Kant, whose categorical imperative directs one to act only on maxims one could will to be universal laws and to treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Other deontological theories include natural rights theories, W. D. Ross's pluralism of prima facie duties, divine command theory, and contractualism. Deontology is one of the three major approaches in normative ethics.
mechanism: Deontology evaluates actions by whether they accord with moral duties and rules rather than by the value of their outcomes. Central to it is the priority of the right over the good: if an act is not in accord with what is right, it may not be undertaken no matter how much good it might produce. This yields constraints, categorical prohibitions on certain kinds of act, such as murdering an innocent person or breaking a solemn promise, that bind an agent even when breaking them would lead to better overall consequences. Deontologists typically treat duties as agent-relative, so that each person has special obligations of their own, and they distinguish doing harm from merely allowing it, holding that actively causing a harm is generally worse than failing to prevent one. Kant's version grounds duty in reason: an action is permissible only if its underlying maxim can be consistently willed as a universal law, and only if it treats rational beings as ends in themselves rather than mere means. Ross's version is pluralistic, positing a plurality of prima facie duties, such as fidelity, gratitude, justice, beneficence, and non-maleficence, each always morally relevant but capable of being outweighed when duties conflict, so that one must weigh them in the particular case. In all these forms, the rightness of an act is settled by its conformity to duty, not by a calculation of consequences.

examples.text: A deontologist may forbid lying or killing the innocent even when doing so would produce better overall consequences.
Kant directs one to act only on maxims one could universalize and to treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means.

variants.name: Kantian deontology
variants.text: The monistic version grounding all duty in the categorical imperative and the demand to treat persons as ends.

variants.name: Ross's pluralism
variants.text: The pluralistic version positing several prima facie duties that must be weighed when they conflict.

whyItMatters: Deontology is one of the three major approaches in normative ethics and a foundational way of thinking about right and wrong, capturing the powerful intuition that some things are simply wrong to do, whatever good might come of them. By grounding morality in duties, rules, and rights rather than in outcomes, deontology gives moral standing to constraints that protect individuals against being used or sacrificed for the greater good, and it underlies the language of human rights, the idea that persons possess an inviolable dignity, and the demand that people be treated as ends in themselves. It offers a principled alternative to consequentialism, resisting the conclusion that any act can be justified if its consequences are good enough, and its concepts, the priority of the right over the good, the distinction between doing and allowing harm, and the weighing of conflicting duties, are central to moral philosophy, law, and applied ethics. Kant's categorical imperative in particular has shaped centuries of ethical thought and the modern conception of moral autonomy.

working.text: determine what moral rule, duty, or right applies to the action in question.
judge the action by whether it conforms to that duty, giving the right priority over the good.
refuse forbidden acts even when they would produce better consequences, and weigh duties when they conflict.

limits: Deontology faces significant objections. Its absolutism can lead to catastrophic outcomes when rules are followed no matter what, most notoriously in Kant's claim that one may not lie even to a murderer at the door asking where an intended victim is hiding, a conclusion many find unacceptable. Deontological theories can generate conflicting duties, giving little clear guidance when two obligations clash, a problem Ross's prima facie duties address only by requiring case-by-case weighing without a fixed rule. There is also the question of where the rules come from and how they are justified. And deontology faces the so-called paradox of deontology, or clean-hands objection: if a certain wrong is bad, it can seem paradoxical that deontology forbids you to commit a smaller wrong to prevent many larger ones, appearing to prize the agent's own moral purity over better outcomes.
misreadings: Deontology does not say consequences never matter at all in life; it says the rightness of an action is not determined solely by its consequences, and that some acts are forbidden regardless of outcome. It is not a single monolithic theory but a family, including Kant's universal-law approach and Ross's plurality of prima facie duties. And it is not obviously correct, since its absolutism, conflicting duties, and clean-hands objection are serious challenges, so treating deontology as ignoring consequences entirely, as one uniform rulebook, or as beyond challenge, misreads a major but contested approach to ethics.
origin: A class of normative ethical theories, one of the three major approaches in ethics, holding that the morality of an action depends on its conformity to duties and rules rather than its consequences; most famously Kant's.
